A griddle is a flat, smooth cooking surface used to cook food by direct heat. Think of it as a wide, thick, metal plate — completely flat on top, with no walls or raised edges (or only very slightly raised edges at the border). You heat it up, place food directly on that flat surface, and cook.

That's the heart of it: flat, smooth, hot, and open.

Imagine a large, heavy, rectangular or round metal slab — almost like a thick metal tile. It's typically made of cast iron or steel, which hold heat very well. It has no deep walls like a pot, and no raised ridges like a grill. Just a wide, even, flat face. It can be as small as a single dinner plate or large enough to cover two stovetop burners at once.

You place the griddle on a heat source (a gas or electric stove burner, or it has its own electric heating coil built in). Once it's hot enough, you spread a little oil or butter on the surface and lay food directly on it. The food cooks from the bottom. When one side is done, you flip it to cook the other side.

Because the surface is completely flat, food makes full, even contact with it — giving it a uniform, consistent cook across the whole surface.

1. Stovetop griddle — A flat metal plate that you place over one or two stove burners. Common in home kitchens. You simply rest it on your stove.

2. Electric griddle — A self-contained appliance with its own built-in heating element. You plug it into a wall socket. It usually has a temperature dial so you can control the exact heat. Popular for home breakfast cooking.

3. Commercial/restaurant flat-top griddle — A large, wide cooking station built into a professional kitchen counter, with burners underneath. This is what you see in diners and fast-food kitchens — the wide, shiny metal surface where cooks make dozens of burgers and eggs at once.
What Gets Cooked on a Griddle

The griddle shines with foods that need a wide, flat surface and steady, even heat. Classic examples:

  • Pancakes and crepes — They need a flat surface to spread out evenly and cook uniformly.
  • Eggs (fried or scrambled)
  • Bacon and sausages
  • Burgers
  • Grilled cheese sandwiches
  • French toast
  • Tortillas and flatbreads
  • Hash browns and sliced vegetables

Basically: anything you'd want browned, crisped, or cooked flat benefits from a griddle.
How a Griddle Differs from Similar Things

This is important, because a griddle is often confused with related cookware.

Griddle vs. Frying pan (skillet):
A frying pan has tall, sloping sides. A griddle has almost no sides. This matters because without sides, it's much easier to flip large, flat foods (like pancakes) with a spatula. A frying pan is better for foods with liquid — sauces, soups, stir-fries — while a griddle is better for flat, solid foods.

Griddle vs. Grill:
A grill has a series of raised metal bars or ridges with open gaps between them. Fat and juices drip down through those gaps, and the food gets the characteristic dark "grill marks." A griddle, by contrast, is solid and flat — no gaps, no ridges. All the juices stay on the surface, and the food gets an even, all-over browning (not striped marks). A griddle is better for delicate foods that might fall through a grill, or foods you want fully browned on the flat side (like pancakes — impossible on a grill).

Griddle vs. Baking sheet (tray):
A baking sheet goes inside an oven. A griddle goes on top of a heat source (a stovetop or its own burner) and is used for direct, open cooking — not oven baking.

If you had to remember just one thing about a griddle: it is flat and smooth. That flatness is its defining feature and the reason it exists as a separate tool. It gives you a wide, open, evenly heated cooking plane — perfect for anything that benefits from a full, direct, flat sear.

A griddle is a flat, smooth, wide metal cooking surface — either a standalone plate placed on a stove, or an electric appliance — used to cook food like pancakes, eggs, bacon, and burgers by laying them directly on the heated surface. It has no walls and no ridges, which makes it different from both a frying pan (which has walls) and a grill (which has ridges and gaps). Its defining purpose is to give food a broad, even, flat surface to cook on.
